passage: Teacher's note, Class 5. I have watched Ankita and Jyoti for several weeks. Jyoti often promises to bring the shared chart paper or to save a seat, then forgets. On Tuesday Ankita heard Jyoti promise again and just said, "Okay," without her usual smile. She then brought her own paper. She still chatted with Jyoti at recess and shared her tiffin, but she no longer waited for her at the gate. I spoke to Ankita privately. She said, "I like her, but I won't trust her with the important stuff." I told her that was a fair choice. I will also talk gently with Jyoti about follow-through.

qa.q: What does Jyoti often promise to bring or do?
qa.a: Jyoti often promises to bring the shared chart paper or to save a seat.

qa.q: What does Ankita's plain "Okay" without her usual smile suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she has stopped believing Jyoti's promises after being let down, though she is still polite.

qa.q: What could Ankita keep doing so she stays careful without being cruel?
qa.a: She can stay friendly at recess and share her tiffin but arrange her own supplies for important things instead of relying on Jyoti.

qa.q: How might Jyoti experience the change in Ankita?
qa.a: Jyoti may notice Ankita is less warm and does not wait at the gate, and could feel hurt or confused until someone helps her see why.

grounding: A teacher's note on a child who, after repeated broken promises, stops relying on her friend for big things but stays friendly.

passage: Valentina had promised to go to the Oslo science museum with Lars on Saturday. She had also promised to return his bike lock, to come to his football match, and to save him a seat at the school concert. She hadn't done any of it. On Saturday morning, when her message came, 'sorry cant make it!! next week promise', Lars didn't feel angry any more. He just felt tired. He replied, 'No worries.' Then he called his neighbour Ole and went to the museum with him instead. On Monday Valentina asked him to help with her poster for Friday's project. Lars helped her at lunch; he liked her jokes. But when she said, 'And you'll bring the glue on Friday?' he said, 'You bring the glue. I'll bring the paper.'

qa.q: Who did Lars go to the museum with?
How did Lars feel when Valentina's message came?
qa.a: Tired rather than angry, worn down by being let down again and again.

qa.q: How does Lars protect himself without being cruel?
qa.a: He stays friendly and helps with her poster, but no longer counts on her for important things like the glue.

qa.q: How might Valentina see Lars's 'You bring the glue'?
qa.a: She might be surprised, noticing that he no longer relies on her promises.

grounding: After repeated broken promises a boy stops counting on his friend for important things while staying friendly.

passage: In the girls' hostel, Madhuri had the only alarm clock in Room 12, and three times she had promised to wake Ayesha for early swimming practice. Three times she had slept through it, and Ayesha had been scolded by the coach for coming late. The fourth night, Madhuri said, 'Tomorrow for sure. Trust me.' Ayesha felt a small, sad hardness in her chest. She smiled and said, 'Thanks, but I'll manage.' Then she asked the warden to lend her a wind-up clock and set it herself. It rang in the dark. Madhuri was snoring. Ayesha tucked Madhuri's blanket back over her foot and went to practice on time. At lunch they still shared pickle and giggled over comics. Ayesha just didn't trust Madhuri with her mornings any more.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when Madhuri said 'Trust me'?
qa.a: Sad and wary; after being let down three times, she no longer believed the promise.

qa.q: How did Ayesha protect herself while staying kind?
qa.a: She borrowed a clock and woke herself, but still shared lunch and jokes with Madhuri.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel if she noticed Ayesha's new clock?
qa.a: Perhaps a bit embarrassed, realising her broken promises had cost Ayesha's trust.

grounding: In a hostel a girl let down repeatedly stops relying on her friend's promises but stays friendly.
